In this guide you'll set up the program and build its content; the sequence and locks come in the next guide. 1 Create a new program In the side menu, click My knowledge hubs and create a new program from the Training programs card. The program management screen has tabs for Layout, Settings, My students, Brand kit, Email campaigns, Analytics, and Meetings. 2 Add courses to the program In the Layout tab, in the Courses in the program strip, click Add course for each course that joins the path. Every course gets a sequence number, and you drag the cards to reorder them. The chain icons between courses mark a lock — more on those in The learning path . The program's course ribbon with the lock icons between them 3 Build chapters and lessons Select a course in the strip, and its content editor opens below: chapters, and within each chapter a lessons table with name, type, source, status, and date. Add new chapter creates a chapter, Add lesson adds a row, and dragging reorders. Each lesson gets a status: Published , Draft , or Hidden . A program chapter with its lessons table 4 Choose lesson types When adding a lesson, pick a type: video lesson , text lesson , quiz — or personal meeting , a one-on-one session with a student that exists only in training programs. A personal meeting slots into the path like any other lesson, and you can mark it as required to continue. 5 Fill in the program details In the Settings tab, under Program details , fill in a name, a short description (up to 200 characters — shown on the program page and in search), a full description, estimated duration, and tags. 6 Set the price and access period Under Pricing , set the program's price and the access period — how long students get access from the moment of purchase: days, weeks, months, years, or forever. Program pricing and access period Good to know The program settings hold a few more options worth knowing: Course workbook — questions that accompany the lessons as students watch, and live sessions with defaults for chat, recording, and cameras. A certificate for the program is marked on screen as coming soon. 7 Publish the program Once the path is built, click Publish program at the top of the screen. The status tag next to the program name updates to "Published". What's next Now turn that list of courses into a real path: The learning path — sequence, locks, and meetings .

title: The learning path — order, locks and meetings
description: How to enforce course order with locks and completion percentages, and how to manage one-on-one meetings with students in your training program
headings: See the locks in the layout
Place a personal meeting in the path
Manage requests on the meetings screen
text: What turns a training program into a real path is the sequence: students advance course by course, with personal check-ins placed along the way. In this guide you'll set up locks, completion percentages, and personal meetings — and see how it all looks from the student's side. 1 Turn on sequential progress In the program's Settings tab, under Course order & locking , flip the Courses must be completed in order toggle — the next course stays locked until the student finishes the current one. The course map shows the chain, and for each course you set the minimum completion percentage required to unlock the next. הגדרת סדר קורסים ונעילה עם מפת הקורסים 2 See the locks in the layout In the Layout tab, lock icons on the links between course cards show where a lock sits. One glance tells you the path is built the way you planned. The program's course ribbon with the lock icons between them 3 Place a personal meeting in the path A personal meeting is a lesson type unique to training programs: when adding a lesson, pick Personal meeting , set a title and duration (15–60 minutes), and optionally mark it Required to continue — the student must hold the meeting to move forward. If a Google Calendar is connected, students book the meeting directly against your availability. 4 Set availability and approvals Under Personal meetings in the settings, turn on the feature and set the rules: calendar connection (Google Calendar or Outlook), maximum meetings per student, meeting duration, and a weekly availability grid where you mark morning/afternoon/evening for each day. The Require approval for booking toggle means every request waits for your approval before it hits the calendar, and you can turn on an automatic reminder an hour or a day ahead. 5 Manage requests on the meetings screen The Meetings tab gathers all the activity: summary cards (this week's meetings, pending approval, monthly total, mentoring hours), a weekly calendar, and a Requests pending approval table where you click Approve or Decline on each request. Clicking a meeting in the calendar opens a panel with the details, the Zoom link, notes, and Send reminder and Cancel meeting buttons — and you can also initiate a New meeting yourself. Meeting requests awaiting the instructor's approval 6 How it looks to students On the student's program dashboard, the learning path map shows the courses as stations: completed, active, and locked. A locked course is marked "Locked" until the completion requirement is met, a "Pick up where you left off" card jumps back to the next lesson, and the upcoming meeting gets its own card with a calendar link. The learning path map as the student sees it Pro tip Switch to student mode (the student/instructor toggle) and walk the path yourself before publishing — especially the locks, which are easy to forget how they feel from the other side. What's next The path is ready. Head back to Setting up a training program to finish the details and pricing, or invite students via Inviting students to a course .

title: Invite students to a course
description: How to add students to a course from the "My students" screen and track their enrollment
text: A course without students is just a draft. In this guide you'll add students to a course manually from the "My students" screen — and see how to track who's joined. 1 Open the course's students screen Go into the relevant course and open My students . Note the course tag above the heading — it tells you which course the list belongs to. 2 Click "Add student" In the corner of the screen's header, click the primary Add student button. The My Students screen header with the Add student button 3 Fill in the student's details Enter the student's details and confirm. 4 Track enrollment The new student appears in the students table. The toolbar above the table has quick-filter tabs — All students , Active , and Leads — each with a counter, so you can see at a glance how many have actually joined. The student table's filter bar — tabs, search, and filtering Good to know Adding students manually isn't the only way: students can join on their own through the course page and the purchase flow. See Pricing your course and Publishing and sharing your course . What the student sees On the other side of the invitation: the student logs in, and the course is waiting for them under "My courses". From there they open the lesson player and start learning — and all their progress updates in your students table. New student on the platform? Point them to the Logging in and starting your first course guide in the student guides. What's next Got students in? Learn to manage them in The My students screen — managing and tracking .

title: The My Students screen — manage and track
description: A tour of the students screen — stats, filtering and search, the students table, per-student actions, and exporting the list
headings: Read the numbers at the top
text: The "My students" screen is your control center for everyone enrolled in the course: who's active, who's stuck, how far each student has gotten — and the actions you can take on each one. In this guide we'll go through the screen section by section. 1 Read the numbers at the top Under the heading sits a row of four metrics: Total students — everyone enrolled in the course Active students — those actually learning Leads — sign-ups who haven't yet become active students Average progress — the average completion percentage across the course Each metric comes with a trend arrow versus the previous period. The My Students screen — metrics, a filter bar, and the student table 2 Filter and search In the toolbar above the table: Tabs — All students , Active , Leads , each with a counter. Search — by name or email. Filter — a button for additional filters. The student table's filter bar — tabs, search, and filtering 3 Read the students table Each student has a row with these columns: Student name , Contact details , Status , Progress (a progress bar with a percentage), Enrollment date , and Actions . Columns with an arrows icon are sortable — click the header to sort by progress, say, and quickly find who's stuck. 4 Take action on a student The actions column in each row has three buttons: View profile (eye icon) — the full student card Send message (envelope icon) — reach out to the student directly Remove student (trash icon) — remove them from the course A student row in the table — view profile, send a message, and remove student Heads-up Remove student disconnects the student from the course. Double-check before removing — details on the consequences in Student settings and access permissions . 5 Export and paginate The Export list button at the top of the screen downloads the student list as a file. At the bottom of the table — pagination: the screen shows part of the list per page, with page navigation and a total count. Pro tip Sort the table by progress, ascending — and the students who most need a nudge float to the top of the list. What the student sees The table data mirrors what's happening on the student's side: the percentage in the progress column is the same number the student sees on their course, and it updates as they complete lessons in the player. A message sent via Send message reaches the student directly. What's next Want to add more students? Inviting students to a course . For control over access and statuses — Student settings and access permissions .

title: Student settings and access permissions
description: Student statuses, approving join requests, removing a student from a course, and alerts for new sign-ups
headings: Remove a student from a course
Stay on top of new sign-ups
text: Who gets in, who sees what, and who's out — in this guide we'll cover the tools that control student access to your content. 1 Understand the statuses In the students table, every student has a status: Active — a student with course access who's actually learning. Lead — a sign-up who showed interest but hasn't become an active student yet. The tabs above the table filter by these statuses, so it's easy to see at any moment who's in and who's on the way. 2 Approve new students In some cases, joining requires your approval — for example, students asking to join a club. Pending requests appear in the "What's waiting for you today" card on the dashboard, with a Review button next to each. 3 Remove a student from a course On the My students screen, in the row's actions column, click the trash icon ( Remove student ). The Remove student button (trash icon) in the table's actions column Heads-up Removing a student cuts off their access to the course. Make sure this is really what you want before confirming. 4 Stay on top of new sign-ups To get an alert for every new student who enrolls in a course, go to your personal profile, and in the Notifications section, turn on the Updates about new students toggle. The 'New student updates' notification toggle in the personal profile Good to know The maximum number of students on your account depends on your plan — from 100 on the Trial plan up to unlimited on the Enterprise plan. Details in the WHITEBOARD plans guide. What's next For day-to-day list management — The My students screen — managing and tracking . To add students — Inviting students to a course .

title: Price your course — one-time, subscription and installments
description: How to set a course price, which payment models exist, and how the price appears to customers on the landing page
text: Before your course goes on sale, you need to decide what it costs and how people pay for it. In this guide we'll cover WHITEBOARD's pricing models, where you set the price, and what the customer ends up seeing. Worth knowing upfront: every sale carries 0% commission — your money stays yours. 1 Open the course settings Go to My knowledge hubs , pick the course, and switch to the Settings tab at the top of the course page. 2 Choose a pricing model Three main models: One-time payment — the customer pays once and gets access to the course. This is the common model for a standalone course. Recurring subscription — a fixed monthly charge. Best suited to a club or a knowledge hub that's constantly updated, where the customer pays each month for ongoing access. Installments — splitting the price into several charges, to lower the barrier to entry on pricier courses. 3 Make sure payments are connected For customers to actually pay, your payment provider needs to be connected to your courses through the official WHITEBOARD app on Make. The full explanation is in Payments and payouts . Good to know WHITEBOARD takes no commission on sales. Payment goes directly through your own payment account, so beyond the credit card company's standard processing fee — every shekel stays with you. What the customer sees The price you set appears automatically in the price box on the course landing page — next to the Join the course now button and the perks that come with the purchase (like lifetime access and a certificate of completion). The price box and join button on the course landing page Clicking the button takes the customer to a secure checkout screen, with the payment methods you've enabled. It's worth opening the landing page after every price change to confirm everything looks the way you intended. What's next Price set? The next step is making sure the page that sells it does its job: Your course landing page , and what the customer meets after the click: The checkout screen — what the customer sees .

title: Your course landing page
description: What's on your course landing page, how to edit it, and how to share the link with customers
headings: Get to know the page structure
Check how it looks on mobile
text: Every course on WHITEBOARD has a landing page — the page potential customers land on before they buy. In this guide you'll see what's on the page, how to edit its content, and how to share it. 1 Open the landing page preview Go into the course via My knowledge hubs and switch to the Brand kit tab. On the preview side, select the Landing page tab — you'll see the page exactly as the customer will, including your brand colors and fonts. 2 Get to know the page structure The page runs top to bottom: Hero section — a background image, rating badge, course name, and a one-line description. Instructor details — photo, name, and title. "What will you learn in this course?" — a bullet list of learning outcomes. Numbers — students, lessons, and rating. Price box — the price, the Join the course now button, and the perks that come with the purchase. A full preview of the course landing page 3 Edit the content Click any text on the page to edit it in place — heading, description, instructor details. In the "What will you learn in this course?" list, add a new bullet with Add point , and remove an existing one by clicking the × next to it. Pro tip Write the bullets as customer outcomes ("You'll be able to build a landing page yourself"), not as a list of topics — that's what sells. 4 Check how it looks on mobile In the preview toolbar, switch between Desktop and Mobile . Most customers will arrive on their phones, so it's worth making sure the headline and price look good there too. 5 Share the page Click Share page — a window opens with the direct link to the landing page. Copy it with Copy and spread it on any channel: social media, email campaigns, or a paid campaign. The landing-page share window with the link to copy What the customer sees Anyone opening the link gets the page exactly as you saw it in the preview — on desktop or mobile, with your brand colors and fonts. They scroll from the headline through the learning outcomes and the numbers, and reach the price box. Clicking Join the course now takes them to a secure checkout screen — and from there, after the purchase, straight into the course. What's next Customer clicked the join button? Continue to The checkout screen — what the customer sees . And if you haven't set a price yet — Pricing your course .

title: The checkout screen — what your customer sees
description: The customer's journey from clicking the join button through payment confirmation and getting access to the course
headings: Payment methods the customer can choose
If the customer starts but doesn't finish
text: When someone clicks Join the course now on the landing page, the purchase flow begins. In this guide we'll walk through what the customer meets along the way — and what you control behind the scenes. 1 From click to payment page The customer clicks the join button on the landing page and moves to payment. The payment itself is processed against your own payment account (CardCom, for example), and the purchase connects to the course through the WHITEBOARD app on Make. 2 Payment methods the customer can choose The payment methods the customer sees are determined by your payment provider — credit card, and depending on your account, Bit, Google Pay, or Apple Pay. 3 What happens right after payment The customer gets immediate access to the course. A welcome email is sent to them automatically, with a button into the course — styled with your brand kit. 4 If the customer starts but doesn't finish Customers who started a payment and abandoned midway aren't lost: the email campaigns system includes an abandoned cart trigger that automatically sends them a reminder email. How to set it up — in The email campaigns system — sequences and triggers . 5 Where you see the transaction Every purchase is logged on the contact's card in the CRM, in the Payments tab — including the amount, payment method, and status. That gives you a complete record of every customer in one place. Good to know WHITEBOARD takes no commission on the sale. What the customer pays goes directly to your payment account, minus only the credit card company's standard processing fee. What's next For payments to work, you need an active payments connection through Make — Payments and payouts .

title: Payments and payouts
description: Connecting payments through the WHITEBOARD app on Make — money is processed in your own account, with 0% commission on sales
headings: Install the WHITEBOARD app on Make
text: On WHITEBOARD, the money never passes through us: payments are processed against your own payment account, and sales carry 0% commission. At this stage there's no built-in payments integration in the platform — the connection works through the official WHITEBOARD app on Make , which links your payment provider (CardCom, for example) to your courses. Good to know How it works in practice: the customer pays at your payment provider ← the provider sends an update (webhook) to your Make scenario ← the WHITEBOARD app adds the customer as a student to the right course. Automatic, end to end. 1 Open a payment account The payment account is yours, directly with the payment provider (CardCom, for example). That's why the money lands directly in your bank account — WHITEBOARD takes no commission on sales; the only deduction is the standard processing fee, like on any transaction. 2 Install the WHITEBOARD app on Make WHITEBOARD has an official app on Make, with a proper guide for connecting courses. You create an API key in the platform and connect it to the app — the whole process is explained step by step in Connecting Make — automations . 3 Build the payments scenario In the Make scenario: a webhook module that receives the payment update from your provider ← routing by the product purchased ← a WHITEBOARD – add student module that adds the customer as a student to the matching course. Here's what a real scenario looks like, routing CardCom purchases to several courses in parallel: You can extend the same scenario to anything you want to happen after a purchase — a WhatsApp message to the customer, a row in your bookkeeping sheet, a community update. 4 Test the pipeline Run a test transaction with your payment provider and confirm the customer was added to the course. In Make you can follow every run of the scenario and see exactly which data came through. What's next The full setup of the Make connection — in Connecting Make — automations . And once payments are working, it's worth checking what the customer sees along the way — The checkout screen — what the customer sees .

title: CRM — all your contacts in one place
description: The central contacts screen — leads, students, and club members in one table with filtering, search, import, and export
text: Everyone who touches your business — a lead who left their details, a student who bought a course, a club member — lives on one screen. In this guide you'll learn your way around the contacts screen: filtering, searching, adding, and exporting. 1 Open your contacts In the sidebar, click My contacts . This opens the central database of all your leads, students, and members. 2 Read the numbers up top The row of cards at the top of the screen gives you a quick snapshot: total contacts, students, club members, leads, and unsubscribes. The summary cards at the top of the contacts screen — total, students, club members, leads, and unsubscribes 3 Filter the list Above the table are quick filter tabs — All , Students , Club members , Leads , Unsubscribes — each with a counter. For more precise filtering, click Advanced filter . 4 Understand the table Each contact shows: Name and an ID number. Email and phone . Type — student, club member, lead, VIP, or canceled. A contact can be several types at once. Source — where they came from: landing page, ads, email campaigns, referral, or direct. Tags — your own free-form labels ("VIP", "Tel Aviv", "hot"). Join date . The contacts table with the filter tabs — types, sources, and tags You can sort by name or join date by clicking the column header. 5 Find someone specific Type a name, email, or phone number in the search field above the table — the list filters as you type. 6 Add, import, and export Three actions sit in the corner of the screen: New contact — manually add a single contact. Import — upload an existing list (say, from a previous email tool). Export — download your data. Everything is available as a full CSV export. Pro tip Tags are the fastest way to build audiences for email campaigns — tag every lead as they come in ("March webinar", "interested in coaching") and you'll thank yourself later. What's next Click a contact to open their full card with all their history — The contact card and timeline .

title: The contact card and timeline
description: A contact's full card — details, quick actions, a timeline of every activity, courses, emails, and payments
text: The contact card brings together everything that's happened with one person: what they bought, what they watched, which emails they opened, and what you agreed on. In this guide we walk through every part of the card. 1 Open the card From the My contacts screen, click the contact in the list. At the top of the card you'll also find general actions: Edit , Send message , and Delete . 2 The profile card The profile sits on the side: name, type badges (student, club member, VIP), email, phone, city, how they joined, and who invited them. Below it — three quick actions: Call , WhatsApp , and Email , plus the tags area where you add a tag with + Tag . A contact's profile card — details, quick actions, and tags 3 The numbers at a glance Four cards sum up the relationship: active courses, average progress, total purchases, and last activity. 4 The timeline The Activity tab shows a timeline of every event, newest first: watching a lesson, opening an email and clicking a link, a payment or subscription renewal, a course enrollment, and notes you've added. This is where you figure out "what's going on with this customer" in seconds. A contact's timeline in the Activity tab — views, emails, payments, and notes 5 The other tabs Notes — write a free-form note and save it with Save note . Every note is stored with the author's name and date. Courses — all the contact's courses with a progress percentage. View details opens a lesson-by-lesson breakdown, and from there you can use Send reminder . The Grant course access button enrolls them in another course at no charge — handy for gifts and one-on-one coaching. Emails — every email sent to them with its status: sent, opened, clicked a link, purchased, or unsubscribed. Payments — a purchase summary and a table of every transaction: date, item, amount, payment method, and status. Heads-up Delete removes the contact along with their entire history. If you just want to stop emailing them — unsubscribe them from the mailing list instead of deleting. What's next Want to send your contacts smart, behavior-based emails? Continue to Email campaigns — sequences and triggers .

title: Mailing home — overview and metrics
description: The mailing home screen — active recipients, emails sent, the activity chart, and recent emails
text: Mailing in WHITEBOARD is its own section — not an external tool, and not a setting buried inside a course. Mailing home is where it starts: who your audience is, what went out recently, and how it did. In this guide you'll get to know the screen and its metrics. 1 Open Mailing In the sidebar, click Mailing lists . The mailing section opens on Mailing home — an overview of all mailing activity in your account, across every list and course. 2 Read the four metrics Four metrics at the top sum up where your mailing stands: Active recipients — how many unique people you have across all lists together. Someone on two lists is counted once. Emails sent — how many emails went out in the last 30 days. Average open rate — the average open rate across all your emails. Average click rate — the share of recipients who clicked a link. The four mailing KPIs on the mailing home — active recipients, emails sent, average open and click Good to know The "active recipients" number is always unique, even when one person appears on several lists. The same logic applies when you actually send — see Mailing lists . 3 Read the activity chart The chart covers the last six weeks. Each week gets two bars side by side: opens (cyan) and clicks (green), with the number printed above each bar. Both metrics sit on the same scale, so the ratio between them is honest and won't mislead you. What you're looking for here is the trend , not a single number. Opens eroding week after week suggest your audience is tiring or your subject lines are repeating themselves. Clicks that stay flat while opens climb suggest the offer inside the email isn't sharp enough. The mailing activity chart — opens and clicks for each of the last 6 weeks 4 Scan recent emails and lists Two cards sit at the bottom of the screen: Recent emails — what went out lately, with the list it was sent to and each email's open and click rates. Click an email to open its email details . An email still in draft opens in the editor instead. My lists — all your mailing lists with their subscriber counts and status (active, automatic, draft). Recent emails and my lists on the mailing home 5 Start a new email The New email button at the top kicks off the sending flow: pick recipients, build in the editor, send. The rest is in Sending an email . What's next Before you fire off your first email, it's worth understanding how the audience gets built — Mailing lists .

title: Mailing lists — building your audience
description: Manual and automatic lists, the list card, your recipient quota, and how duplicates get merged across lists
headings: Get to know the lists screen
text: A mailing list is an audience — a group of people who get an email together. Before you write your first email, it's worth understanding the two kinds of lists and the rule that stops one person from getting the same email twice. 1 Get to know the lists screen The screen splits in two: the rail holds all your lists, grouped by type, and the center opens whichever one you selected. At the top of the rail you'll see the summary — how many lists you have and how many people are in them altogether. The mailing lists screen — the manual and automatic lists rail beside the selected list 2 Two kinds of lists Manual lists — you decide who's in. Good for an audience that signed up for something specific: live session registrants, newsletter subscribers, workshop signups. Automatic lists · by behavior — lists the system maintains on its own from a condition, marked with an Automatic tag. For example course students for a specific course, or cart abandoners — people who started checkout and didn't finish. They keep themselves current: a new student joins automatically, and anyone who no longer meets the condition drops out. Pro tip An automatic list is always up to date as of the moment you send. You never need to refresh it or import people into it. 3 Read the list card Click a list and it opens in the center of the screen with its description, status, and four metrics: subscribers , emails sent , open rate , and click rate — so you see how this audience behaves, not just how big it is. Below that: where subscribers came from, and every email sent to the list with its own open and click rates. You can also start a New email straight to this list from here. A mailing list card — subscribers, emails sent, open rate and click rate 4 Your recipient quota At the bottom of the rail you'll find your plan's recipient quota — how many unique recipients you have right now against the quota, and how many are left. The quota counts unique people, not rows across lists. 5 Everyone gets exactly one email This is the principle that makes lists safe to use. A person can be on both "Weekly newsletter" and "Course students". When you send one email to both lists, the system merges the duplicates and sends them one email . So: The summary at the top of the rail is a count of unique people, not the sum of the lists. When you pick recipients to send to, you'll see the deduplicated number alongside how many duplicates were merged. Go ahead and pick overlapping lists without a second thought — nobody gets a double. What's next Audience ready — head to Sending an email . To manage individual people and their timelines, see CRM — all your contacts .

title: Sending an email — recipients, editor, send
description: The three steps of sending — picking recipients with duplicates merged, subject and preheader, and sending now or on a schedule
text: Sending an email is three steps: pick who, build the email, send. In this guide you'll walk the whole path end to end — no in-between screens, no hidden settings. 1 Pick recipients Click New email (from Mailing home or from inside a list) and the recipient picker opens. Lists are grouped into manual and automatic, and you can tick one, a few, or Select all . There's a search box too, for when the rail gets long. At the bottom of the screen sits the live summary: how many recipients you've selected, and next to it how many duplicates were merged. The count is always deduplicated — anyone on several lists gets one email. Choosing recipients — selecting lists and the deduplicated count at the bottom Good to know A list that hasn't been published yet (0 recipients) shows greyed out and can't be selected — so you won't accidentally send to an empty audience. Click Continue to editor . 2 Write the subject and preheader At the top of the editor sit the three fields that decide whether your email gets opened at all: The recipients bar — who this is going to and how many recipients. A Change recipients link takes you back to the picker. Email subject — what people see in their inbox. Preheader — the preview line next to the subject. Optional, but it's one more place to earn the open. The email editor head — recipients bar, subject line and preheader 3 Build the body Below the fields is the email canvas, built from blocks. Full details in The visual email editor . Your work saves automatically, so you can leave and come back. 4 Send now or schedule When the email is ready, click Continue to send . A summary dialog opens with: Recipients — the lists you picked, the final recipient count, and how many duplicates were merged. When — Send now , or Schedule and pick a date and time. Confirm, and the email goes out or joins the scheduled queue. The send dialog — recipients summary, merged duplicates, and immediate or scheduled sending Heads-up An email that's gone out can't be pulled back. If you're not sure about the copy, use Send test from the editor and send yourself a copy first. What's next Once it's out, track how it did in Email details . Want BOARDi to write the email for you? See Creating a campaign with BOARDi .

title: The visual email editor
description: Build an email from blocks — headings, images, buttons, and personalization variables — with a preview and a test send
text: WHITEBOARD's email editor works in blocks, just like building a lesson: add a heading, text, an image, or a button — without touching code. In this guide you'll build the body of the email, after the recipients and subject are already set in Sending an email . 1 Get to know the editor In the center is the email itself, exactly as the recipient will see it. At the top of it sit the subject and preheader fields, and above those, the recipients bar. Your work saves automatically as you go (an "Auto-saved" indicator at the top), so you can leave and come back without losing anything. 2 Add blocks Click Add content block or pick a block from the side drawer. The blocks include: main heading and subheading, body text, quote, divider, CTA button, image / GIF, spacer, social links, personal signature, course/product card, image + text, copy box / coupon, image gallery, countdown timer, and an address-and-contact-details footer. The email editor block drawer — every content type you can add Pro tip The course/product card block automatically pulls in the image, name, and price of a course you pick from the platform — the fastest way to sell a course inside an email. 3 Reorder and delete Every block has a small toolbar that appears when you click it: move up, move down, delete. Editing happens in place — click the text and type. 4 Drop in personalization variables Inside your text, use variables like {{recipient name}} — they're swapped for each recipient's real value, so everyone gets a personal email. 5 The unsubscribe block always stays Every email has an unsubscribe block at the bottom. It's required and can't be deleted — that way you stay compliant with email rules without thinking about it. 6 Save blocks to reuse Set up a signature or a social links block that shows up in every email? Save it as a personal block — it'll be waiting in the Mine tab of the block drawer in every future email. 7 Check before you send Preview — see the finished email, and switch between desktop and mobile views. Send test — send a real copy to any address you choose; variables are filled with sample values. Always send yourself a test before the real thing — an email that's gone out doesn't come back. What's next Email ready? Click Continue to send and finish up in Sending an email .

title: Creating a campaign with BOARDi
description: Build an email in conversation with BOARDi — goal, campaign type, behavior targeting, tone, and your own writing voice
text: You can build an email yourself in the editor, or you can build it in a conversation. The mailing BOARDi asks you a few questions — what the goal is, who it's for, what tone — and assembles both the audience and the email. In this guide you'll walk through that conversation step by step. 1 Pick a goal BOARDi opens by asking what the email needs to achieve, with four goals: Win back students — people who bought a course and disappeared. Launch a course / session — invite your audience to something new. Nurture and content — a tip or ongoing value for the list. Update / announcement — tell everyone something important. The goal drives everything after it: which audience BOARDi proposes and which writing framework it picks. The mailing BOARDi asks what the email should achieve — four goals to choose from 2 Campaign type Next you choose between two types: Single scheduled email — one message. Send now or schedule it for a date and time. Recurring email sequence — a series that goes out automatically, like a win-back sequence or a welcome sequence. 3 Target by behavior This is where BOARDi builds your audience from real behavior instead of a hand-made list. The main filter is students who haven't logged in for more than 7 / 14 / 30 days, for a specific course or across all courses. You can layer on more conditions: Joined before a date / Joined after a date Cart abandoners — started checkout and didn't finish You can also just describe the audience in your own words in the chat, for example "students who haven't logged into Calm Parenting for two weeks". 4 Check the audience it built The rail on the side shows the audience in real time: every source, how many people it holds, and how many duplicates were merged. This audience is dynamic — it keeps updating until the moment you send, so if a student comes back to watch before then, the list reflects it. The audience BOARDi built — 223 unique recipients with 6 duplicates merged Good to know The same rule holds here: someone who appears in several sources gets one email only . The count in the rail is always deduplicated — see Mailing lists . 5 Tone and writing voice BOARDi asks which tone fits the audience — warm and personal , brief and to the point , or upbeat and energetic . Then it offers to learn your voice : upload a sample of copy you've written, or skip it and let BOARDi learn from the emails you've already sent through WHITEBOARD. Samples shape tone, structure, and length — not just word choice. 6 Review the draft At the end BOARDi shows you the finished email, and from that same window you can: Preview — see the email as the recipient will see it. Send test — send a real copy to your own address. Open in editor — keep working on the blocks by hand in the email editor . Pro tip BOARDi is a starting point, not a substitute for your judgment. Always read the copy before sending — especially numbers, dates, and prices. What's next Happy with the draft? Move on to sending and scheduling in Sending an email .

title: Email details — reading the results
description: The metrics of a sent email — delivered, opened, clicked, unsubscribed — plus the per-list breakdown and link performance
text: Once an email goes out, the email details screen is where you see what happened to it: how many landed, how many opened, what people clicked, and who unsubscribed. In this guide you'll read the screen and decide what to change next time. 1 Open the email details From Mailing home or from a list card, click a sent email. At the top you'll see the subject line, the send date and time, and the lists it went to. From here you can also Preview it, Duplicate it into a new email, or Send to another list . 2 Read the five metrics Sent — how many recipients it went out to in total, and to how many lists. Delivered — how many emails actually arrived, and the delivery rate. A low rate points to bad addresses or a sender problem. Opened — the share and number of recipients who opened. Clicked — the share and number who clicked a link. Unsubscribes — how many asked to leave the list, and what share of recipients that is. The five metrics of a sent email — sent, delivered, opened, clicked and unsubscribed Good to know Always read delivery before opens. If delivery is low, the open rate is misleading — the problem is technical, not your copy. Sender details and domain verification live under Settings → Email settings , see Your account's global settings . 3 Compare your lists The breakdown by list table shows how the exact same email performed in each list separately, plus the combined total. This is the most useful comparison on the screen: same copy, same moment — so a gap between lists tells you about the audience, not the email. A list that lags consistently needs its own copy, or it's simply gone cold. Breakdown by list — how the same email performed in each list separately 4 See what people clicked Link performance lists every link in the email and how many recipients clicked it. This is where you find out whether your main button did the work, or a side link stole the attention instead. Below it, recipient activity shows exactly who opened and who clicked what. Link performance — which link in the email was clicked 5 Decide what to change Three common readings: Low opens — the problem is the subject line or the send time. Try something more concrete. High opens, low clicks — they opened but weren't convinced. Sharpen the offer and the button. High unsubscribes — frequency or fit. Make sure the audience that got it was the right one, and see Mailing lists . What's next Head back to Mailing home to see the trend across six weeks — a single email is a dot, the trend is the story.

title: Build an exam
description: Build a multiple-choice exam step by step — questions, correct answer, passing grade, time limit, and video references for wrong answers
headings: Point wrong answers to a lesson clip
text: An exam in WHITEBOARD checks that your students actually understood the material — and can even block progress in the course until they pass. In this guide you'll build a complete exam: questions, grading settings, and a smart reference back to the lesson for when a student gets it wrong. 1 Open the exam editor Enter the exam from the course structure in the knowledge hub. At the top of the screen you'll see the Edit mode bar with a Draft status, an Auto-saved indicator, and a Publish button. You edit the exam name right in the title. 2 Set the exam rules In the settings bar, you define how the exam behaves: Passing grade — drag the slider to the percentage you want. Blocking exam — students can't continue the course until they pass. Retakes — unlimited, or 1 to 5. Show answers — whether students see the correct answers at the end. Shuffle questions — random question order for each student. Time limit — turn it on and set the minutes. The exam editor's settings bar — passing score, blocking, retakes, and time 3 Write the questions Click Add question , type the question text and the answer options. Mark the correct answer by clicking the circle next to it. You can add an option with Add option , delete an option (at least 2 are required), drag questions to reorder, and delete an entire question. A question card in the exam editor — answer options and marking the correct answer 4 Point wrong answers to a lesson clip For every question you can set a lesson reference : pick a lesson from the course and type a timestamp (min:sec). When a student gets the question wrong, instead of just seeing the correct answer — they watch the relevant clip from the lesson that explains it. Watch clip lets you make sure you picked the right moment. Link to lesson — a wrong answer points to an explained video clip Pro tip Video references turn an exam from measurement into learning — the student who got it wrong goes right back to the exact point they missed. 5 Review and publish Preview shows the exam from the student's point of view. When everything's ready, click Publish — the status changes from Draft to Published and the exam is available to students. Your changes are saved automatically the whole time you're editing. Heads-up Deleting a question is immediate and can't be undone. If you're on the fence — better to edit the wording than to delete. What the student sees Students reach the exam from their learning path and get an opening screen: the number of questions, the passing grade, and the time limit — and if the exam is blocking, a clear warning: "You must pass this exam to advance to the next lesson". They click Start exam and answer question by question, with a progress counter, a timer, and Previous / Next navigation. Before submitting there's a confirmation — after submitting, there's no going back. The exam start screen for the student — exam details and the blocking warning At the end, students see their grade in a big ring with a full question review — their answer next to the correct one. Passed? A "Next lesson unlocked" banner and a To the next lesson button. Failed? They see how many attempts remain, which lessons are worth revisiting, and on every wrong question you set a reference for — a Watch the explanation from the lesson card that plays the exact clip. The student's results after failing — remaining attempts and a 'watch the explanation from the lesson' card What's next Students have started taking the exam? Head to Exam results — the instructor's view . Want to award a certificate at the end? Certificates — templates and issuing .

title: Exam results — the instructor view
description: The instructor's results screen — averages, student table, problem-question analysis, and export
text: Once your students have taken the exam, the results screen pulls the whole picture together: who passed, who failed, and which questions are tripping up too many students — a sign the question, or the lesson, could use sharpening. 1 Open the results screen Enter the exam in the knowledge hub and switch to the Results view. The top bar shows the exam status ( Published ) and how many students have taken it, and an Edit button takes you back to the exam editor. 2 Read the key metrics Four cards at the top of the screen sum up the exam: Average grade , Passed , Failed (out of total test-takers), and Highest grade . The exam results key metrics — average, passed, failed, and top score 3 Go through the student table The Student results table shows each student's grade, status (passed/failed), attempt number, and exam date. Click a column header to sort, and the view icon on a student's row to see their exam. The student results table — score, status, attempt, and date 4 Spot problem questions The Question analysis panel shows the percentage of correct answers for each question. A question with an especially low success rate gets a Problem question tag — a hint that the wording is confusing or the material wasn't covered enough in the lesson. Question analysis — pass rates and flagging a problem question Pro tip A problem question is an opportunity: add a reference to the relevant lesson clip — so a student who gets it wrong goes straight back to the explanation. 5 Export the results At the bottom of the screen: Export results to download the data, and Send results by email . What's next Want to ask free-form questions about student performance across the whole course? BOARDi's student analyst does exactly that.

title: Certificates — templates and issuing
description: Pick a certificate template, set a signature and issuing conditions — and see what students get when they finish
text: A completion certificate gives students a reason to make it to the end — and something to be proud of afterward. In this guide you'll pick a template, customize the content, and decide when the certificate is issued automatically. 1 Open the certificate tab Enter the knowledge hub and switch to the Certificate tab. The screen we saw in the design belongs to a training program, alongside tabs like Layout, Settings, and Email campaigns. 2 Choose a template The Choose certificate template gallery has four templates: Classic , Modern , Professional , and Creative . Your brand kit — colors and logo — is injected automatically into every template, and a live preview on the side updates with each choice. The certificate template gallery — Classic, Modern, Professional, and Creative 3 Customize the certificate content In the Certificate settings card, you set: Custom text — the sentence that appears above the student's name (for example, "Proudly awarded to:"). Instructor signature — drag in a signature image or type the instructor's name. Certificate settings — custom text, signature, issuing criteria, and QR 4 Set the issuing conditions Check off what's required for the certificate to be issued: Completed all courses in the program , Passed all exams , and you can also add Attended all one-on-one meetings . You can also turn on Include verification QR — a QR code on the certificate that lets anyone verify it's authentic. Click Save certificate settings , and Full preview shows the certificate at full size. What the student sees When a student meets the conditions, they get a celebratory screen with their certificate: name, issue date, serial number, signature, and QR. From there they can Download PDF , share on LinkedIn or WhatsApp , and see a summary of what they completed in the program. The certificate the student receives — PDF download and sharing on LinkedIn and WhatsApp Good to know Every certificate carries a unique serial number, so even without the QR, any issued certificate can be identified. What's next The issuing conditions lean on exams — make sure yours are built right in Building an exam . The overall look is set in the course brand kit .

title: The games in the platform and how to add them
description: Meet WHITEBOARD's three games — Word Search, Memory, and Hangman — and how they fit into your course
headings: Understand where a game lives in the course
text: Games are a way to reinforce what's been taught without it feeling like an exam. WHITEBOARD has three built-in games — Word Search, Memory, and Hangman — and each one lives inside a knowledge hub as part of the course structure, with content you define. 1 Meet the three games Word Search — students hunt for words from the material in a letter grid, against the clock. You set the word list, the grid size, and the search directions. Full guide: The Word Search game — building and editing . The Word Search game from the student's perspective — the letter grid, the timer, and the word list Memory — a pairs game of hint and answer: flip cards and look for matches, like a term paired with its definition. A hint can be text or an image. Full guide: The Memory game — building and editing . The Memory game from the student's perspective — the card board and attempt counters Hangman — students guess a word from the material letter by letter, with a mistake limit and an optional hint. There's scoring and rounds. Full guide: The Hangman game — building and editing . The Hangman game from the student's perspective — the word, the keyboard, and the score 2 Understand where a game lives in the course A game is a content item inside a knowledge hub — it sits in the course structure alongside lessons and exams, and students reach it from their learning path. In the breadcrumbs you'll see it like this: Knowledge hubs → course name → Game. 3 Fill the game with content Each game has its own editing screen where you define the words, the pairs, and the settings — time, size, hints, and more. There's a dedicated guide for each game: Word Search , Memory , Hangman . Pro tip A good game leans on terms students have already met in the lessons. 8–15 words or pairs is usually enough for one round. What's next Pick a game and dive in: the Word Search game is a good starting point. For the bigger picture of content items — Lesson types .

title: The Crossword game — build and edit
description: Build a Word Search — word list, grid size, search directions, and timer — and see how students play it
text: WHITEBOARD's Word Search is exactly what it sounds like: students get a grid of letters and hunt for words from the material, against the clock. It's great for reviewing key terms — you just set the word list and the system builds the grid. This guide covers the editing screen and what the student sees. 1 Open the Word Search editor Enter the game from the course structure in the knowledge hub and switch to editing. In the breadcrumbs you'll see: Knowledge hubs → course name → Game: Word Search → Edit. 2 Set the game settings In the settings bar at the top, you set: Game time — 30, 60, 90, or 120 seconds. Grid size — 8×8, 10×10, 11×11, or 13×13. Directions — horizontal, vertical, and diagonal. Any combination works. The Word Search editor — time, grid, and direction settings, plus the word list Pro tip A big grid + diagonals = a hard game. For beginners, stick with 8×8 and horizontal and vertical only, then dial up the difficulty later. 3 Build the word list In the Word list area, type one word per card. The word counter updates as you go. Add words with Add word and delete with the trash icon on the card. Heads-up Deleting a word is immediate. Make sure the list is complete before you save. 4 Review and save Preview shows the grid generated from your words with the word list beside it — that's how you confirm everything fits. When you're happy, click Save game . What the student sees Students open the game from the course's learning path and get an opening screen — click or press the spacebar to start. From there: the letter grid in the center, and beside it a Time left timer, a Found counter, and the Words to find list. At the end of a round they can click Play again . The Word Search game from the student's perspective — the letter grid, the timer, and the word list Capabilities The grid is built automatically from your word list — no arranging letters by hand. Difficulty control through grid size, directions, and time. A pressure timer with a one-click rematch. What's next Want a game that drills understanding, not just recognition? Try the Memory game — pairs of term and definition.

title: The Memory game — build and edit
description: Build a Memory game of hint-answer pairs — text or image, grid size, time limit, and shuffling — and see how students play it
text: The Memory game drills matching: students flip cards and look for pairs of hint and answer — say, a term matched with its definition, or a picture matched with its name. This is the game that practices understanding, not just word recognition. In this guide you'll build a complete Memory game. 1 Open the Memory editor Enter the game from the course structure in the knowledge hub and switch to editing. In the breadcrumbs: Knowledge hubs → course name → Game: Memory → Edit. 2 Set the game settings In the settings bar: Game name — the title students will see. Grid size — 3×4 (6 pairs), 4×4 (8 pairs), or 4×5 (10 pairs). Time limit — turn it on and set the minutes, or leave it open-ended. Shuffle cards — a random order every time the game opens. The Memory game editor — hint–answer pairs and grid settings 3 Build the pair list In the Pair list area, each row is a pair of hint and answer : Choose the hint type — Text or Image (for an image, click Upload image ). Type the hint and the answer. Add pairs with Add pair — up to the number of pairs your chosen grid can hold. Pro tip Image hints level up the game in visual fields — design, photography, anatomy: a picture on one side, the term on the other. 4 Review and save Preview opens the game exactly as the student will see it, and Save game saves your changes. What the student sees Students get a board of face-down cards, with Attempts , Pairs , and Time counters at the top. They flip two cards per turn looking for a match; once all the pairs are found, a finish screen appears with a star rating and stats, plus a Play again option. The Memory game from the student's perspective — the card board and attempt counters Capabilities Hint-answer pairs in text or image, in any combination. Three grid sizes to control game length. An optional time limit and card shuffling on every open. A finish screen with stars — students love beating their score. What's next The third game in the arsenal: Hangman — letter-by-letter word guessing with hints.

title: The Hangman game — build and edit
description: Build a Hangman game — words and hints, maximum mistakes, timer, and publishing — and see how students play it
text: In Hangman, students guess a word from the material letter by letter, with a limited number of mistakes and a hint to point the way. The game works great for professional vocabulary — each word comes with a hint that's really its definition. This guide builds the game end to end. 1 Open the Hangman editor Enter the game from the course structure in the knowledge hub and switch to editing. In the breadcrumbs: Knowledge hubs → course name → Game: Hangman → Edit. At the top of the screen there's an Edit mode bar with a Draft / Published status. 2 Set the game settings In the settings bar: Game time — 30, 60, 90, or 120 seconds. Maximum mistakes — 5, 7, or 9. Show hint — whether students see the hint next to the word. The Hangman editor — words and hints, max mistakes, and the publish bar Pro tip 5 mistakes with the hint showing is a good balance for beginners. Want a challenge? 5 mistakes with no hint — but only for words that were actually taught. 3 Build the word list Each row in the list holds a word + a hint . Type away, add rows with Add word , and delete whatever you don't need. Heads-up Deleting a word is immediate. Save only once the list is complete. 4 Review, save, and publish Preview shows the game, Save game saves it. To make the game available to students, click Publish — the status changes from Draft to Published , and you can switch back to draft anytime. What the student sees Students open the game, press the spacebar to start, and get the word as blank lines, an on-screen Hebrew keyboard, a hint (if you turned it on), and Round and Score counters. Every wrong guess advances the drawing; at the end, a results screen appears with a New game option. The Hangman game from the student's perspective — the word, the keyboard, and the score Capabilities A word + hint per row — the hint turns guessing into review of the material. Difficulty control: number of mistakes, time, and whether the hint shows. Rounds and scoring — students move on to the next word within the same round. A Draft / Published mechanism — edit in peace and publish when it's ready. What's next For an overview of all three games and how to place them in a course — The games in WHITEBOARD .

title: Schedule a live session
description: How to schedule a live session — details, prepping interactive content in advance, settings, and inviting students
headings: Invite participants and send the invitation
text: A live session starts long before you go on air. On the scheduling screen you set when it happens, prep polls, questions, and games in advance, and send invites to your students — so on the day itself, all that's left is to click and start. 1 Open the scheduling screen Enter the course through My knowledge hubs and open the live session scheduler. 2 Fill in the session details In the Schedule a new live session form, fill in: Session name and a description (optional). Course / program — which course the session belongs to. Date and start time . Estimated duration — from 30 to 120 minutes. Maximum number of participants . The form for scheduling a new live session 3 Prep interactive content in advance Next to the form is the Interactive content prep area. You can pick a ready-made preset — a template you built ahead of time in the preset library (say, "Standard lesson — poll + 3 questions + game") — or prep items manually: Prepared polls — a poll question with options. Live questions — a question with the correct answer marked. Games — Memory, Hangman, or Crossword. Everything you prep here will be waiting for you in the live room, ready to send with one click. Preparing interactive content in advance — polls, questions, and games Pro tip Better to build your polls and questions now, not mid-broadcast — during the live session itself you'll want to be with your students, not your keyboard. 4 Set the session settings Under Session settings , toggle on or off: Record automatically — the session records from the start. Allow chat and Allow raise hand . Mic muted on entry — students join muted. Send a reminder — an hour before or a day before. 5 Invite participants and send the invitation Under Invite participants , choose between All course students and Manual selection of specific students. Click Create live session , check the details in the confirmation window, and click Send invitation — every student gets a message with a direct link to the session. The session confirmation window before sending the invite You can also save the session as a draft and come back to it later. What's next The session is scheduled — now it's worth getting to know The instructor's live room .

title: The instructor's live room
description: A tour of the live room — video and screen sharing, participant management, chat, recording, and ending the session
headings: Control your camera, mic, and screen share
text: The live room is where the live session actually happens: this is where you see your students, share your screen, answer in chat, and launch the interactive tools. This guide walks through every area of the screen, so your first broadcast feels like home turf. 1 Get your bearings The live room has four areas: Top bar — session name, timer, participant counter, recording indicator (REC), and the End session button. Video stage — your main video, with a participant gallery below it and a mic indicator for each student. Sidebar — three tabs: Participants , Chat , and Interactions . Bottom bar — the quick controls. The instructor's live room — an overview Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-room-overview) 2 Control your camera, mic, and screen share The bottom bar holds the Microphone , Camera , and Screen share buttons. When screen sharing is active, a "Screen sharing active" indicator appears and your video moves to a small window (PiP), so students keep seeing you. The bottom control bar — mic, camera, screen share, and record Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-room-bottom-bar) 3 Manage participants The Participants tab shows everyone present, with search and a raised hand (✋) next to anyone asking to speak. Clicking a participant opens an actions menu: Mute Make presenter Remove from session The sidebar in the live room — participants, chat, and interactions Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-room-sidebar-tabs) 4 Answer in chat The Chat tab holds the session's written conversation. Your messages are marked as the instructor's, so you can answer questions without pausing your explanation. 5 Record If you checked Record automatically when scheduling, recording starts on its own and the REC indicator lights up in the top bar. You can also start and stop recording manually with the Record button in the bottom bar. After the session, your recordings are waiting on the Live recordings screen. 6 End the session Click End session (in the top bar or the bottom bar). A confirmation window appears: all participants will be disconnected and the recording saved automatically. Heads-up Ending the session disconnects all students immediately. Make sure you're really done — there's no way to "return" to the same broadcast. What's next The tools you send students mid-broadcast have guides of their own: Live polls and questions , Breakout rooms in a live session , and Playing a game live .

title: Polls and questions in a live session
description: Quick polls and live questions with points and a leaderboard — how to send them mid-broadcast and what students see
headings: Build and send a quick poll
Watch the results in real time
Build a live question with points
text: A poll and a live question are the fastest way to take the room's pulse mid-broadcast: a poll gathers opinions with no right answer, while a live question tests knowledge — with points, a timer, and a leaderboard. Both are sent from the live room and pop up for students on top of the video. 1 Open the Interactions tab In the live room sidebar, click Interactions (or Interactive tools in the bottom bar). From the tools grid, pick Quick poll or Live question . The interactive tools grid in the live room Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-tools-grid) 2 Build and send a quick poll In the poll panel, fill in: The poll question . Options — four by default, and you can add more with + Add option . Duration — 15, 30, or 60 seconds. Click Send poll — and it appears for every student. The quick-poll builder panel in the live room Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-poll-teacher-panel) 3 Watch the results in real time While the poll is running, the panel shows a response counter ("Responses: 14 / 28") and percentage bars updating live. When it's over, click Close poll — that's the perfect moment to talk through the results with everyone. 4 Build a live question with points In the Live question panel, write the question and the answers, and mark the correct one by clicking the circle next to it. You'll also set: Timer — 10 to 30 seconds. Points — how much a correct answer is worth. Click Send question . As students answer, you'll see the response counter, the answer breakdown, and the leaderboard . The live-question builder panel — correct answer, timer, and points Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-quiz-teacher-panel) Pro tip A few live questions in a row with points becomes a full-on competitive quiz — and if you do it regularly, it's worth saving the sequence as a ready-made preset . What the student sees The poll or question pops up for the student as a card on top of the video, without leaving the broadcast. For a poll — the options with voting percentages, a "Your vote has been recorded" confirmation, and the time remaining: A quick poll as students see it, over the video Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-poll-student-view) For a live question — a countdown timer, answers A–D, and after answering, a points indicator ("+100 points!") and their personal spot on the leaderboard ("3rd out of 28"): A live question on the student's side — answers, points, and leaderboard Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-quiz-student-view) Capabilities Polls with a flexible number of options and live results in percentages. Live questions with a correct answer, timer, points, and a cumulative leaderboard. Prepping polls and questions in advance — on the scheduling screen or as a preset . What's next Want a bigger competition than a single question? Try Playing a game live .

title: Breakout rooms in a live session
description: Splitting the broadcast into small breakout rooms — automatic or manual assignment, timer, messages to all rooms, and returning to the main room
headings: Set up rooms and assign participants
text: Some discussions just don't happen in front of 28 people. Breakout rooms split the broadcast into small groups for a set amount of time — each group in its own video room — then bring everyone back to the main room to continue the lesson. 1 Open the breakout rooms window In the live room sidebar, under the Interactions tab, click Breakout rooms . The management window opens with all your participants. 2 Set up rooms and assign participants In the settings row: Number of rooms — how many groups you'll have. Assign automatically — the system spreads participants evenly. Assign manually — drag participants between rooms yourself. Discussion time — 5 to 30 minutes. Each room can get its own name (say, "Warm colors"), and anyone not yet placed appears in the Unassigned area — drag them into the right room. The breakout rooms window — splitting participants into rooms Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-breakout-modal) 3 Open the rooms Click Open breakout rooms — participants move to their rooms and the timer starts running. Next to each room you'll see its status (active / waiting) and its participant count. 4 Move between the rooms You're not stuck on the outside: Join next to any room drops you in — to listen, steer, and answer questions. Send a message to all rooms — a broadcast message that appears in every room at once (say, "Two minutes left"). 5 Bring everyone back When time's up, click Return to main room — all participants come back to the main broadcast, and you can wrap up what came out of the groups. Pro tip Give each room a defined task before you split — a group that knows what's expected of it starts talking in the first second, not the fifth minute. What the student sees The moment you split, the student gets a transition screen: "You've been moved to a breakout room," with the room name, its participant count, and the time remaining. Inside the room they see only their own group members, a Back to main room button, and a note that the instructor will bring them back when the discussion ends. A breakout room on the student's side — the room name, participants, and time left Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-breakout-student-view) Capabilities Automatic assignment or manual drag-and-drop, with an "Unassigned" area. Custom names for each room and a shared timer for all of them. Instructor can join any room, plus broadcast messages to all rooms. What's next Breakout rooms can also be planned ahead inside a ready-made preset — so the split is ready before the broadcast even starts.

title: Presets — ready-made templates for your broadcast
description: Live lesson kits — building a ready-made sequence of polls, questions, and games and reusing it in every broadcast
text: If you build the same sequence of interactions before every broadcast — an opening poll, a few questions, a wrap-up game — live lesson kits (presets) save you the trouble. Build the sequence once, save it as a kit, and use it in every live session. 1 Open the kit library Under Live sessions , go to Ready-made kits . Each kit appears as a card with a description, the number of items, and how many times you've used it. From here you can edit , duplicate, or delete a kit. The live session kits library 2 Create a new kit Click Create new kit . Give it a name and a short description — they're what will help you recognize it later in the kit list on the scheduling screen. 3 Add items to the sequence In the kit editor, click Add item and choose from the menu: Poll — an opinion question with options. Live question — a question with a correct answer, timer, and points. Games — Memory, Hangman, or Crossword. Timer and Breakout rooms . Each item appears as a card in the Items in kit list: clicking it opens the full details (the question, options, and correct answer), and the drag handle changes the order. The kit editor — items in sequence and a preview 4 Check the sequence in preview The Preview panel shows the kit as a timeline — item after item — along with an estimated duration and interaction count. Run preview plays the sequence just as your students will experience it. 5 Save and use Click Save kit . From now on it's available in two places: On the scheduling screen — pick it in the Ready-made kit field while prepping the session. In the live room — the prepped items wait in the Interactions tab, ready to send in the order you set. Pro tip A card with the Default tag is the kit that loads automatically. Duplicating an existing kit is the fastest way to build a variation — change a question or two instead of starting from scratch. What the student sees The kit itself is invisible to students — they simply meet its items during the broadcast, one after another: a poll popping up over the video, a question with a timer, a game with a leaderboard. For how each item looks on their end, see Live polls and questions and Playing a game live . Capabilities Any sequence of polls, live questions, games, timers, and breakout rooms. Drag to reorder and a preview of the whole sequence. Kit duplication, a default kit, and usage tracking ("Used 12 times"). Heads-up Deleting a kit can't be undone. If you just want a different version — duplicate instead of deleting. What's next Built a kit? Schedule your next broadcast with it — Scheduling a live session .

title: Play a game in a live session
description: Launching a Memory, Hangman, or Crossword game mid-broadcast — with a timer, leaderboard, and live tracking
headings: Pick a prepared game or create a quick one
text: A game mid-broadcast is an energy break that also teaches: the whole class plays at once on the same board, with a timer and a live leaderboard. Three types are available — Memory, Hangman, and Crossword. 1 Open the game tool In the live room sidebar, under the Interactions tab, click Game . 2 Pick a prepared game or create a quick one In the game panel: Game type — Memory, Hangman, or Crossword. Choose a prepared game — one you built in advance (say, through the scheduling screen or a preset ). Create a quick game — or fill in word and hint pairs on the spot. Set the duration (one to 5 minutes) and click Start game . The game-launch panel in the live room Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-game-teacher-panel) 3 Follow the game live The game appears over the broadcast for everyone. You see the game board, the timer, and how many participants are playing — alongside a leaderboard updating live and a stats bar (pairs found, attempts, who's leading). An active live game — the game board, timer, and leaderboard Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-game-overlay) 4 End the game When time runs out — or when you click End game — everyone returns to the regular broadcast. It's a great moment to give the leaders a shout-out and revisit the terms that came up in the game. Pro tip A Memory game with term-definition pairs makes an excellent lesson recap — students review the material without feeling like they're reviewing the material. What the student sees The game opens for the student on top of the video: the game board in the center, the timer and participant count up top, and next to the board a leaderboard where their own row is highlighted ("You"). Every correct match earns points and climbs the table. The game on the student's side — the game board and leaderboard Screenshot from the platform — coming in the capture phase (live-game-student-view) Capabilities Three game types: Memory, Hangman, and Crossword. A library of prepared games alongside quick game creation mid-broadcast. Timer, live leaderboard, and a progress bar for the instructor. What's next Games can also go into recorded lessons, not just live sessions — see The games on the platform and how to add them .

title: Live session recordings
description: Where live session recordings are stored and how to watch, download, and share them
text: Every live session you recorded is waiting for you after the broadcast on the course's recordings screen. From there you can rewatch, download, share a link with anyone who missed it — and see how many students have already watched. 1 Open the recordings screen Enter the course through My knowledge hubs and open Live session recordings . At the top of the screen you'll see the recordings counter, with a search field next to it. 2 Find the recording Each recording appears as a card with a thumbnail, duration, date, participant count, and view count. Search by name in the Search recording... field. The list of live session recordings 3 Watch and navigate by chapters Clicking a recording opens it in the side player. Below the player you'll find chapters with timestamps — clicking a chapter jumps straight to that moment in the recording. The recording player — chapters, download, share, and the BOARDi transcript 4 Download or share Two buttons sit below the player: Download recording — the video file saves to your computer. Share link — a viewing link you can send to students who didn't make it. 5 Read the transcript At the bottom of the player is the BOARDi transcript — a text transcript of the session. Handy when you want to quickly find a quote or a topic without scrubbing through the video. Heads-up Deleting a recording (the delete button on the card) can't be undone. Make sure you've downloaded a copy if you'll need it. What's next Want your next live session to feel truly live? Go over Live polls and questions and Presets — ready-made templates for live sessions .

title: The analytics screen — the metrics that matter
description: Your course's viewing, progress, and activity metrics — how to read them and what to do with what you find
headings: Drill down to the individual student
text: The course analytics screen brings together everything happening in your course: who's watching, how far students are getting, and where they get stuck. In this guide we'll go through each area of the screen and what you can learn from it. 1 Open the course analytics Go into the course via My knowledge hubs and select the Analytics tab. 2 Pick a date range In the corner of the screen, choose the period: today, last 7 days, last 30 days, 3 or 6 months, the current year — or a custom range. The whole screen updates accordingly. 3 Read the four main metrics At the top of the screen are four cards, each with a change indicator: active students, average rating, lesson views, and total watch time. The four main metrics in the course analytics — active students, rating, views, and watch time 4 Views over time The chart shows two lines — views and sign-ups — across the period. A spike in sign-ups without a spike in views? Worth checking that your welcome email is actually getting people into the first lesson. 5 Find where students get stuck Two areas complement each other: Student progress — a distribution: how many finished, how many are midway, and how many barely started. Completion by lesson — each lesson's completion rate. A sharp drop between one lesson and the next is the clearest sign of a drop-off point: maybe the lesson is too long, maybe too hard. The views and student-progress charts in the course analytics Next to them, Popular lessons ranks your lessons by views — so you know which content works best. 6 Drill down to the individual student The Student activity table shows each student's progress, lessons completed, last seen, and status. A student who hasn't logged in for two weeks — a natural candidate for a reminder email. The student activity table — progress, lessons, and last login 7 Export the data The Export button at the top of the screen downloads your data — everything is available as a full CSV export, for analysis in any external tool. Pro tip You don't have to read the charts on your own — just ask BOARDi "where are students dropping off the course?" and get an answer straight from your data. See the student analyst . What's next Want your marketing data (campaigns, pixel, site traffic) in the picture too? Continue to Connections and data sources .

title: Connections and data sources
description: Where BOARDi and analytics get their data — what's active from day one and which external sources you can connect in one click
headings: Check how much of the picture BOARDi sees
text: The insights BOARDi shows you are built on data sources.
